title: Where the Sun stops setting
hook: In June the far north gets a Sun that never sets. Where exactly does that start?

knows: that days are long in northern summer
that the Earth's axis is tilted
doesNotKnow: the latitude where the Sun stops setting on the solstice
that it is 90 degrees minus the tilt

misconception: The Sun stays up all day only at the poles, or only well past the Arctic Circle.
objective: The learner can explain that on the June solstice the Sun does not set north of 90 - 23.4 = 66.6 N, because the night side's edge stops that far short of the pole.

claims.text: On the June solstice the Sun does not set north of about 66.6 N, which is 90 degrees minus the tilt of about 23.4 degrees; the reveal places it between the highest latitude where the learner saw a sunset and the lowest where they saw none (computed by dayHours() in Demo.tsx).
claims.source: Day length from cos(H) = -tan(lat) tan(dec) with dec = 23.44 (obliquity, IAU / Astronomical Almanac, from memory): H reaches 180 degrees (24 h of day) when lat >= 90 - 23.44 = 66.56. Geometric centre of the Sun, airless spherical Earth. Computed in Demo.tsx. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node of dayHours(): 24 h first at 66.56 N (66.5 gives 23.42 h; first 0.1 slider step with 24 h is 66.6); 90-23.44 = 66.56 shown as 66.6. Since sets < 66.56 <= never, the reveal's line always lies between the two quoted latitudes. Obliquity 23.44 (IAU 2006: 23.4393 at J2000) correct to my knowledge.

claims.text: In this model, at 65.0 N the solstice day is 21 h 07 min long.
claims.source: Same formula, lat = 65: cos(H) = -tan 65 x tan 23.44 = -0.931, H = 158.6 degrees, day = 2H/15 = 21.1 h. Computed live in Demo.tsx (scratch b.mjs agrees: 21.12 h). | 2026-10-14 (v6, build 6 phone fit, demo-builder): the Daylight readout moved from a readout row into the day strip's top line ('Daylight 21 h 07 min', same fmtDay); claim text and value unchanged, status left as is.

claims.text: The line at 66.6 N is the Arctic Circle.
claims.source: The Arctic Circle is defined as the parallel at 90 degrees minus the obliquity, about 66.56 N today (Astronomical Almanac; any atlas). From memory, not checked online. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): learner-visible reveal sentence changed to cm-geography's W-266 text; needs a fresh check. Claim wording unchanged; the reveal sentence now reads 'That line is the Arctic Circle, not the Tropic of Cancer (23.4°N), ...'. | FC pass 29 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-269): LEFT UNVERIFIED, not disputed. Stage check passes: the reveal's 'That line is the Arctic Circle' follows P1's 'The line between is about 66.6°N' (LINE = 90 - 23.44 = 66.56, shown 66.6; node). The claim is a naming convention and rests on a reference (Astronomical Almanac / atlas) that I could not open this session (web fetch fails DNS; search snippets are not an opened source). Previous verification was from memory. Needs a fact-checker re-check with an opened reference. | FC pass 31 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-275): VERIFIED against an opened reference. WordNet 3.1 (Princeton), npm wordnet-db 3.1.14 (tarball sha256 9b93831a...e79a), dict/data.noun, opened and read locally in the session scratchpad, not added to the project: synset 08513808 Arctic_Circle = "a line of latitude near but to the south of the north pole; it marks ... the southernmost point at which the midnight sun can be seen on the northern summer solstice"; midnight_sun (11502979) = "the sun visible at midnight (inside the Arctic or Antarctic Circles)". The stage computes exactly that line: dayHours() first gives 24 h at 66.56 N (LINE = 90 - 23.44, shown 66.6°N), so the line the reveal names is the line WordNet defines. claims.text: Because air bends sunlight and the Sun is a disc, the real midnight Sun can be seen a little south of the line.
claims.source: Standard sunrise/sunset is defined at a Sun-centre altitude of -0.833 degrees (34 arcmin refraction plus 16 arcmin semi-diameter; USNO / Astronomical Almanac). With that, the solstice midnight Sun reaches roughly 65.7 N. From memory, not checked online; the lesson gives no number for it. | WITHDRAWN 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): cm-geography cut the no-air caveat from the reveal; no learner-visible sentence carries this claim now (the stage caption keeps only 'Toy: no air', a model label). Fact-checker to confirm the withdrawal. | FC pass 29 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-269): WITHDRAWAL CONFIRMED. Demo.tsx v4 read on every path: no learner-visible sentence says air bends sunlight or that the midnight Sun is seen south of the line. The caption 'Toy: no air' is a model label, not this claim.

claims.text: 23.4 N is the Tropic of Cancer, where the Sun is directly overhead at noon on the June solstice; the Arctic Circle is a different line. The north has its longest day around June 21 (predict question).
claims.source: Standard geography references (Tropic of Cancer at the Sun-declination limit of about 23.44 N; June solstice about 21 June). · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: VERIFIED. Tropic latitude = solar declination limit (23.44 N); on the June solstice the subsolar point is at the declination, so noon Sun is overhead there. "June 21": the solstice falls on June 20-22 depending on year and time zone; declination one day off the solstice differs by 0.0035 deg, so day length differs by seconds. Suggest "around June 21" if the builder touches the text. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): learner-visible reveal sentence changed to cm-geography's W-266 text; needs a fresh check. Reveal now carries the Tropic as a clause; 'around June 21' per pass 19. | FC pass 29 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-269): DISPUTED. The stage makes two claims different from the text. (1) The predict question reads 'June 21 is the longest day in the north.' with no hedge; the claim says 'Around June 21'. Opened source: astronomy-engine 2.1.19 Seasons() (npm tarball, read and run locally) puts the June solstice at 2024-06-20 20:51 UTC and 2028-06-20 20:02 UTC (June 20 in UTC; in the Americas in more years), so the flat date is false in some years. Fix: 'Around June 21 the north has its longest day.' (2) The reveal clause 'the Tropic of Cancer (23.4°N), where the noon Sun is overhead' drops 'on the June solstice': read alone it says the noon Sun is always overhead there. astronomy-engine: noon zenith distance at 23.44 N is 0.00 on 2026-06-21, 1.35 deg on 06-01, 23.2 deg at the September equinox. Fix: '..., where the noon Sun is overhead that day.' (+2 words, about 83, under 90). The numbers hold: solstice Sun declination 23.436-23.439 (2000-2028), shown 23.4. Also, the Tropic of Cancer name is a convention whose reference I could not open; after the fix this needs a re-check with an opened reference. | Reworded W-274; FC pass 29 dispute resolved in text, pending opened-reference re-check (W-275). | FC pass 31 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14, W-275): ALL CHECKS PASS, LEFT UNVERIFIED ON INDEPENDENCE ONLY. Stage: predict 'Around June 21 the north has its longest day.' and reveal '...not the Tropic of Cancer (23.4°N), where the noon Sun is overhead on the June solstice.' match the claim. Opened: WordNet 3.1 (Princeton), npm wordnet-db 3.1.14 (tarball sha256 9b93831a...e79a), dict/data.noun, opened and read locally in the session scratchpad, not added to the project: tropic (08692883) = "either of two parallels of latitude about 23.5 degrees ... the points farthest north and south at which the sun can shine directly overhead"; Tropic_of_Cancer (08693276) = "about 23 degrees to the north of the equator"; summer_solstice (15246808) = "June 21, when the sun is at its northernmost point". astronomy-engine 2.1.19 (npm tarball sha256 605e9e9e...9cdd), run locally: June solstice 2024-2030 falls 06-20 20:51 to 06-21 14:11 UTC, Sun dec 23.435-23.439 (shown 23.4); noon zenith distance at 23.44 N on 2026-06-21 is 0.002 deg. Hold reason: the predict sentence 'Around June 21 the north has its longest day.' is the fact-checker's pass-29 wording adopted verbatim (W-274 ruling 1); per the W-258 independence precedent the fact-checker does not verify wording it drafted. Evaluation-steward to rule (W-280). | FC pass 32 (fresh fact-checker instance, 2026-10-14, W-284, under the W-280 ruling): VERIFIED. Artifact first; my own installs, scripts and numbers. astronomy-engine 2.1.19 (installed into the scratchpad): June solstice 2020-2030 falls 06-20 20:01Z to 06-21 14:57Z; Sun dec 23.4348-23.4390; highest Sun altitude at 23.436 N, 0 E on 2026-06-21 is 89.956 deg (overhead); 50 N day length peaks on Jun 21 (16.1480 h vs 16.1474 on Jun 20 and 16.1470 on Jun 22). Opened: WordNet 3.1 (wordnet-db 3.1.14, which I downloaded myself, sha256 9b93831a...e79a, matching the hash): tropic 08692883, Tropic_of_Cancer 08693276, summer_solstice 15246808. claims.text: On the June solstice the north pole leans 23.4 degrees toward the Sun, so the night side's edge stops 23.4 degrees short of the pole (the orange gap on the globe); a town whose daily circle fits inside the gap stays lit all day.
claims.source: The night side is the 90-degree circle centred on the antisolar point at 23.44 S; along its meridian it reaches 90 − 23.44 = 66.56 N, leaving 23.44 degrees to the pole. Geometry in Demo.tsx (night, gap). Reveal paragraph 2. | Added 2026-10-14 (v3) by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node: a 90-degree circle centred at 23.44 S reaches at most 66.56 N, on the antisolar meridian, leaving 23.44 degrees to the pole; any parallel above it is wholly lit. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v4, W-266 by demo-builder): learner-visible reveal sentence changed to cm-geography's W-266 text; needs a fresh check. recall.question: If the Earth's axis were tilted 30 degrees instead of 23.4, where would the June midnight Sun begin?
recall.why: The night side's edge stops one tilt short of the pole, so the Sun stops setting at 90 minus the tilt: 90 - 30 = 60 N.
